resumen: What goes in the photo and what stays out: get closer, check the edges and leave room where it's needed.

bloques.alt: Two photos of the same scene, a person standing. On the left, the photo taken from far away: the person looks small, there is too much space and a pole sneaks in at the right edge. A dashed rectangle marks what the photo on the right shows. On the right, the photo taken up close: the person fills the photo and there is nothing else.
bloques.pie: 1 From far away: too much space and a pole. 2 Up close: the subject fills the photo and there is nothing extra.

bloques.texto: Framing is deciding what goes in the photo and what stays out. Almost always, it gets better when you move closer.

It is common to leave too much empty space by not getting close enough. Move closer to the subject, or use the zoom if you can't: it is clearer what the photo is about and you cut what distracts. If the background tells something, keep a little. On a phone, move closer yourself before using digital zoom, as in “Zoom and lenses: which to use”.

Before you shoot, scan all four edges, not just the center: look for poles, branches, people or colors that compete with the subject. And don't cut a person at the joints (wrists, elbows, knees, ankles): either keep them whole or cut clearly somewhere else.
Don't always shoot horizontal: try vertical too and choose according to what you want to show and where you'll see it (for example, vertical looks good on a phone and on social media).

items: Leave more space in front of something that moves, or of where a person looks, than behind it: it seems to have somewhere to go.
A natural frame, like a door, a window, an arch or some branches, surrounds the subject, makes it stand out and adds depth.
Leave a margin around it: you can crop or change the format later, but you can't add what you didn't capture.

bloques.texto: Pick an object at home. Take a photo from far away, another getting close until it fills the photo, and another in vertical. Before each shot, check the four edges.
